title: Qubit CSS codes with Universal Transversal Gates
authors: Arpit Dua, Adam Holmes, Michael J. Gullans, Victor V. Albert
abstract: The Eastin-Knill theorem rules out a universal set of transversal logical gates on any code that detects single-qubit errors. The theorem constrains one partition of the qubits at a time. We show that depth-one layers of few-qubit gates, each respecting its own partition, can together generate a universal logical gate set on an error-correcting code. Each logical gate generator is then a single depth-one layer followed by error correction of the same stabilizer code, with no magic-state distillation, code switching, gauge fixing, lattice surgery, or other gadgets. We show that such codes can be found by applying an entangling circuit to a lower-distance "seed" code admitting a depth-one non-Clifford gate and an appropriate "kernel" code. We construct 47 codes with depth-one generating sets that tolerate at least one faulty gate per layer, including a [[37,1,7]] and a [[59,1,9]] code, both of check weight at most eight.
summary: This paper develops methods to achieve universal gate sets for quantum computation by utilizing depth-one layers of few-qubit gates, circumventing constraints from the Eastin-Knill theorem. The authors construct numerous suitable codes using a seed-kernel coupling technique and rigorously analyze the fault-tolerance and circuit depth of these systems. This work provides significant theoretical blueprints for building scalable, fault-tolerant quantum processors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitations imposed by the Eastin-Knill theorem, which restricts universal transversal logical gates on single-error-detecting codes.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a universal logical gate set can be generated using depth-one layers of few-qubit gates, each respecting a different qubit partition, without requiring complex gadgets.
method: They construct these generators by coupling a lower-distance 'seed' code to an ancillary 'kernel' code using entangling circuits (Seed-Kernel Construction).
model_or_system: The work focuses on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (CSS codes) used for fault-tolerant quantum computation, analyzing specific constructions like the tesseract and Carbon codes.
key_observables: The construction yields 47 codes with depth-one generating sets, and the circuit distance ($d_{	ext{circ}}$) of the Q37 code was calculated to be 7.
important_parameters: The fault tolerance condition requires $d \geq 2\ell+1$ for $\ell$-fold transversal gates; error rates are analyzed based on gate error $p$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on a conservative fault model, and the simulation of failure probability uses heuristic decoders like the Tesseract decoder.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the compilation of logical gates from depth-one layers (Figure 1), the general seed-kernel coupling framework (Figure 3), and the schematic structure of the Q37 extraction round (Figure 5).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical necessity of depth-one layers to constructing specific codes via seed-kernel coupling, and finally analyzing the circuit depth and failure probability of a concrete example like Q37.
why_interesting: The rigorous construction of universal gate sets using only depth-one layers is a major theoretical advance for fault-tolerant quantum computation, providing concrete pathways around known theoretical limitations.

(a) A logical gate compiled from depth-one layers, each made of disjoint gates on at most ℓqubits of one partition of the qubits (horizontal lines), with error correction between layers. Gray layers are Clifford, and the teal layer U2 is non-Clifford. The layers of any one partition generate a finite logical group whenever every part has fewer than d qubits, but layers on several partitions can generate a universal one. (b) Distance against length for the 47 codes of Table I, whose ℓ-fold transversal generators satisfy ℓ≤⌊(d −1)/2⌋, so that at least one faulty gate per layer is correctable. The color gives ℓand the symbol the number k of logical qubits.
